documents.abstract: Hybrid Intelligence for Industrial Process Optimization: Establishing the Need Presentation delivered at the 23rd International Conference on Informatics in Control, Automation and Robotics (ICINCO 2026) within the Special Session on Hybrid Artificial Intelligence (HybAI 2026) held in Angers, France, October 26–28, 2026. Summary:Over 80% of industrial artificial intelligence proofs-of-concept (PoCs) stall or fail to reach production due to a fundamental structural mismatch: physical plants operate under rigorous thermodynamic and hydraulic conservation laws with zero fault tolerance, whereas pure data-driven machine learning models act as unconstrained black boxes omitting causal mechanisms. This presentation opens the HybAI 2026 Special Session by surveying the theoretical and practical imperatives for Hybrid Intelligence: Limits of Pure Data-Driven AI: Why the No Free Lunch theorem and severe physical exploration budgets make learning physics ab initio sample-inefficient and hazardous in production. Critique of Sutton's "Bitter Lesson": In digital games, simulation and trial-and-error exploration are computationally free; in municipal water systems and heavy industry, unconstrained exploration destroys hardware (pipe bursts, pump cavitation). Physical invariants are indispensable inductive scaffolds, not bottlenecks. Lessons from Neurorobotics: How biological motor control decomposes known morphological kinematics from state-dependent disturbance estimation, providing a direct design template for industrial gray-box digital twins. Acausal Physics & Differentiable SciML: Unifying Differential-Algebraic Equations (DAEs) with adjoint sensitivity analysis to guarantee safety and sample efficiency by design. Official Publication Citation:Lippi, V. and Johard, L. (2026). Hybrid Intelligence for Industrial Process Optimization. In Proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on Informatics in Control, Automation and Robotics (ICINCO 2026) - Volume 1, pages 869–876. documents.abstract: Natural disasters increasingly cause severe casualties, displacement, and economic destruction, yet emergency response operations are routinely hindered by fragmented inter-agency coordination, resource planning bottlenecks, and information limited to overwhelmed traditional communication channels. To address these operational challenges, this chapter presents the Intelligent Holistic Emergency Logistics Platform (iHELP), a cloud-based simulation-optimization system designed to coordinate multi-modal supply chains and provide real-time situational awareness during emergencies. Abstracting the challenge as a multi-commodity, multi-mode transportation problem, iHELP models the assignment, routing, and scheduling of heterogeneous vehicle fleets across ground, air, and maritime networks under dynamic operational constraints. To overcome data scarcity during emergencies, iHELP incorporates a dedicated Social Media Analytics Module that uses natural language processing, computer vision, and spatial clustering to ingest user posts, filter misinformation, compute confidence metrics, and infer urgent humanitarian needs. Additional integrated modules manage weather disruptions, service prioritization, and infrastructure availability. Decision-makers interact with the system via a web dashboard that visualizes animated operations, transporter utilization, and inventory trends. Developed and validated in collaboration with NATO’s Crisis Management and Disaster Response Center of Excellence through simulated flood response scenarios, iHELP demonstrates strong capability in delivering robust, high-quality emergency logistics plans under stress and uncertainty.

Diabetic retinopathy can be screened (assisted by artificial intelligence) in primary care and underserved contexts, and technical accuracy is irrelevant to whether patients and practitioners consider the service a legitimate offer.This secondary qualitative research study explored how trust, data ownership and equity are formed in empirical descriptions of AI-assisted retinal screening.A systematic search found 35 sources from 2016-2026.The findings were based on sixteen major articles published since 2021, whereas a different body informed the introduction, theoretical framework, research gap, methods and discussion of literature.This yielded three themes suggested by reflexive thematic synthesis: trust as a relational goal and not an assurance of accuracy alone; retinal data ownership is an open relationship of governance; equity is a dilemma of increased access and risk redistribution.Speed, convenience, and instant outcomes were well-regarded by patients, although this consideration faded as AI seemed to substitute clinical elucidation or reuse of data was opaque.Practitioners were open to AI when accountability, escalation channels, and training could be perceived, but raised anxieties over consent, accountability, information security, and skewed model performance.The greatest gains in access were most effective when AI was integrated within attainable care pathways, though inaccessible images, referral failure, digital savvy, and subgroup bias could recreate disparity.The paper finds that reliable AI eye screening entails human-controllable communication, purpose-driven data stewardship, and equity considerations throughout the screening process, not just at the algorithmic endpoint.The analytic focus is therefore multi-actor and system-level, integrating patient experience with practitioner readiness, institutional accountability, data governance and referral capacity.

documents.abstract: This study proposes an organizational and economic framework for improving ERP-based integrated management in industrial enterprises, with particular emphasis on Uzbekistan's machinery manufacturing sector. It examines opportunities to enhance the integration of information systems, strengthen coordination among procurement, warehousing, and production operations, and improve the adaptability of conventional static inventory management policies. The proposed framework combines the integration of existing Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) functions, multi-model bills of materials (BOMs), feedback from Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES), dynamic calculations of safety stock and reorder points, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted decision support under human supervision. An economic optimization model incorporates inventory holding costs, procurement costs, material shortage costs, and costs associated with production interruptions. Static and dynamic inventory management policies are compared using operational and economic performance indicators. The study presents a conceptual framework and an analytical evaluation methodology; empirical validation at the enterprise level requires actual production, inventory, and procurement data.

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Many spinal imaging reports are written above recommended health literacy levels, limiting patient comprehension at a time when rapid electronic access to radiology results is increasing. We aim to evaluate whether supplemental natural language processing (NLP)–modified radiology reports—within the context of usual patient portal access to the original report—are associated with improved patient-reported perceived understandability compared with standard reports among patients undergoing spine imaging. METHODS: This is a prospective randomized controlled study with limited participant blinding, conducted with 2 spine surgeons affiliated with a single academic medical center in New York City. Participants (18 years or older) undergoing spine imaging at initial surgical consultation were enrolled and were randomized to receive either their original radiology report or a supplemental NLP–modified version. Radiology reports were rewritten using a standardized natural language processing prompt (ChatGPT 4.0) and reviewed for accuracy by study investigators. The primary outcome was survey-based patient-reported perceived understandability. Secondary outcomes included objective readability scores (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, Flesch Reading Ease, Simple Measure of Gobbledygook, Gunning-Fog Index). RESULTS: Fifty-two adults were enrolled; 42 (81%) completed the postintervention survey. Among 52 randomized participants (26 women [50%]), NLP–modified reports demonstrated significantly improved objective readability across all indices compared with original reports (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, 5.9 ± 1.1 vs 11.0 ± 1.7; Reading Ease, 71.0 ± 10.3 vs 28.2 ± 12.5; Simple Measure of Gobbledygook, 20.1 ± 12.7 vs 23.5 ± 15.7; Gunning-Fog Index, 8.2 ± 1.1 vs 14.3 ± 1.8; all P < .01). Of 42 survey respondents, those receiving supplemental NLP-modified reports reported greater ease of understanding the report language (4.2 ± 1.2 vs 2.6 ± 1.5, mean-difference 95% CI: 0.75-2.53, P < .01, Bonferroni-corrected- P = .02), and less difficulty with medical terms (2.0 ± 1.5 vs 3.6 ± 1.4, mean-difference 95% CI: −2.51 to −0.60, P < .01, Bonferroni-corrected- P = .04). CONCLUSION: Supplemental NLP-modified radiology reports were associated with improved objective readability and higher patient-reported perceived ease of understanding in a spine surgery initial consultation setting. These findings support further investigation of NLP-generated supplemental explanations within supervised clinical workflows.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: In modern times, artificial intelligence (AI) is considered one of the most important technological revolutions in the industrialization process. Artificial Intelligence technologies are widely used to digitize, automate, and increase the efficiency of production. The basis of the “Industry 4.0” concept is precisely artificial intelligence, big data, robotics, and internet technologies. In this regard, studying the applications of Artificial Intelligence in the industrial field is relevant both theoretically and practically. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming various industries by providing new solutions, increasing efficiency, and reducing costs. Artificial Intelligence (AI) refers to the development of computer systems that can perform tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as learning, problem solving, perception, decision making, and language understanding. Artificial Intelligence systems use various techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and computer vision to analyze large amounts of data and make predictions or decisions based on that analysis. Some examples of AI applications include virtual personal assistants, self-driving cars, image and speech recognition, and medical diagnostics and treatment. AI is a rapidly developing field and can transform many industries and aspects of daily life. Applications of AI in the industrial field are accompanied by automation of production, energy saving, increased safety, and the creation of new technological capabilities. In the future, the competitiveness of industrial enterprises will be measured precisely by the level of use of AI technologies.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Formative assessment is widely regarded as a cornerstone of students’ academic achievement, but its implementation at the classroom level is jeopardised by inconsistent guidelines. This study examined the influence of formative assessment guidelines on students’ academic achievement in public secondary schools in Kigoma Municipality, Tanzania. The study employed a convergent research design under a mixed-methods approach to collect data from 169 respondents. A total of 156 students were selected using simple random sampling, six teachers experienced in using formative assessments, six academic masters/mistresses, and one education officer. Data were collected using questionnaires for students and interviews for educators. The quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics (frequencies, percentages, and means) using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) version 20 with a tested reliability coefficient of 0.713, while qualitative data were analysed using a deductive content analysis approach. The findings indicate that students valued weekly tests and clear teacher instructions as motivating and fair mechanisms that enhanced students’ academic achievement. Teachers also reported that classroom assessment guidelines are useful, but the guidelines lack competence-based clarity. Further, students prioritise formative assessments over national examinations, while socioeconomic limitations undermine the effectiveness of take-home assignments. The study concludes that the use of formative assessment guidelines improves academic achievement, but challenges in teacher preparation and policy-practice alignment persist. The use of technology in formative assessment is limited by infrastructure and connectivity; additionally, the study concludes that increased use of artificial intelligence and the internet is not a feasible option for public secondary schools in Kigoma Municipality. Therefore, policymakers should emphasise capacity-building initiatives for teachers and administrators in competence-based curriculum assessment methods. The shift from traditional teaching and learning approaches to competence-based models is often hindered by resource constraints or shortages. Emphasis on critical thinking should begin at the classroom level and support students’ academic achievement rather than merely high grades in final assessments.

The article examines innovative digital banking technologies as a key factor in the transformation of modern banking activities and the modification of traditional banking business models. The contemporary technological foundations of digital banking are considered, including artificial intelligence and machine learning, Big Data and data analytics, cloud technologies, APIs and Open Banking, robotic process automation, digital identification, modern payment technologies, and blockchain. Current trends in the digitalization of the Ukrainian banking sector are analyzed, including the development of cashless payments, the increasing adoption of contactless and tokenized payment instruments, the expansion of digital payment infrastructure, the formation of a regulatory framework for Open Banking, and the growing use of artificial intelligence technologies. It is substantiated that the digital transformation of banking activities is comprehensive in nature and involves a gradual transition from technological modernization to business process automation, personalized customer service, and the transformation of banks’ business models. The main transformational effects of innovative technologies are systematized, including increased operational efficiency, reduced service delivery time, expanded accessibility of financial products, improved customer experience, enhanced quality of managerial decision-making, and improved risk management systems. The key challenges of digital transformation are identified, including cyber risks, data protection, technological dependence, model risks associated with the use of artificial intelligence. The necessity of assessing the effectiveness of digitalization not only in terms of the scale of technology adoption but also according to its economic, customerrelated, operational, and risk-related effects is substantiated. The promising areas for the development of digital banking in Ukraine are identified, including the wider application of artificial intelligence, the development of Open Banking and Open Finance, the formation of digital ecosystems, the expansion of embedded finance, cloud technologies, and intelligent automation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and data analytics are reshaping marketing practice, yet many universities in emerging economies have been slow to reflect these changes in their curricula. Limited digital infrastructure, inadequate faculty expertise, and concerns about the ethical use of AI continue to constrain curriculum reform. This study develops the DigitalReady Marketing Education Framework (DRMEF) to guide the integration of AI and data analytics into marketing education. Drawing on a conceptual theory-building approach, the study synthesizes literature on AI, marketing education, technology adoption, and digital competency development. The analysis shows that effective integration depends on four closely connected elements: digital infrastructure, curriculum redesign, faculty capability, and ethical AI governance. The framework highlights that preparing graduates for data-driven marketing requires more than technology adoption; it also demands institutional commitment and continuous curriculum development, offering a practical guide for higher education institutions in emerging economies.
topics: Information Systems Education and Curriculum Development
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Islamic educational institutions are increasingly drawn into a technological moment shaped by artificial intelligence and, more quietly, by quantum physics, yet little research asks how either can be woven into Islamic pedagogy without unsettling tawhid, the epistemological commitment underlying the tradition. This PRISMA-guided systematic review maps the opportunities, challenges, and design principles for integrating AI and quantum physics into Islamic education and proposes a working framework. Of 1,563 unique records retrieved from five databases (2016-2025), 57 studies were retained: 48 engaging directly with an Islamic-education context (Stream A), and 9 general quantum-physics-education studies included deliberately as a comparison corpus (Stream B), since none met a joint Islamic-context-and-quantum criterion. AI is used mainly for personalised Qur'anic and Arabic-language learning and administrative efficiency; quantum content remains almost entirely confined to secular STEM curricula. Data privacy, algorithmic bias, teacher readiness, and decontextualised content recur as concerns. The review proposes the AI-Quantum-Islamic Education Framework (AIQIEF), grounding adoption in tawhid-based epistemology rather than treating these technologies as neutral add-ons.

This study investigates the effectiveness of integrating ChatGPT within genre-based pedagogy to strengthen critical thinking in ESP (English for Specific Purposes) academic writing among students in East Java higher education institutions. Using a mixed-methods sequential explanatory design, the research involved 142 students from six private universities.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming spine care by enabling analysis of imaging, clinical, and textual data to support diagnosis, risk stratification, and treatment planning. Techniques including deep learning–based image analysis, radiomics, and natural language processing (NLP) offer opportunities to standardize interpretation and derive quantitative biomarkers beyond human visual assessment. This narrative review examines recent innovations in spine-focused biomedical informatics and evaluates their clinical relevance and translational challenges. A narrative review was conducted, focusing on AI in spine care across imaging, radiomics, NLP of electronic health records, and clinical decision support. Literature was selected via targeted PubMed searches; studies describing technical development, validation, and clinical implementation were synthesized, addressing explainability, uncertainty, workflow, and regulation. Convolutional neural networks enable vertebral and disc segmentation, detection of degenerative and traumatic pathology, and quantitative assessment of paraspinal musculature. Radiomics approaches extract high-dimensional imaging features that improve the prediction of osteoporosis, fracture risk, tumor characterization, and surgical outcomes. NLP techniques, including emerging large language models, unlock clinically relevant information from unstructured text, enhancing outcome prediction and population-level analyses. Multimodal clinical decision support systems integrating imaging, EHR data, and NLP-derived features demonstrate promise for personalized risk assessment and treatment guidance. Challenges remain regarding data heterogeneity, generalizability, privacy, and prospective validation. AI-driven biomedical informatics holds substantial promise to enhance diagnostic accuracy, prognostication, and personalized decision-making in spine care. Successful clinical translation will require robust validation, explainable, uncertainty-aware models, regulatory alignment, and integration into clinical workflows to ensure safe, trustworthy, and patient-centered adoption.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Mental health education for university students faces challenges, like inadequate personalization and delayed intervention. This study develops an intelligent platform integrating artificial intelligence and big data. The platform comprises structured courses, an artificial intelligence psychological assistant, self-assessment tools, and personalized recommendation functions, with core logic centered on resource classification, optimization, and dynamic mining. A quasi-experiment was conducted with 386 undergraduates for eight weeks, followed by a three-month follow-up. Results show the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group in mental health literacy, help-seeking attitudes, and emotional regulation self-efficacy (p < 0.001), with effects persisting long-term. Platform usage intensity positively moderated intervention effects, and high-engagement users gained the most. This study verifies the platform's effectiveness in optimizing mental health information resource management, providing a feasible digital solution for university mental health education.

Background and objective: Nursing faculty have been hesitant to incorporate artificial intelligence into coursework due to various reasons, including the risk of affecting academic integrity and the potential for receiving inaccurate information. As nursing cohorts continue to grow, innovative approaches are needed to meet learning objectives; such as artificial intelligence. Incorporating artificial intelligence into group projects may increase responsible, ethical, and critical use of artificial intelligence and support programs in managing larger cohorts. The purpose of this initiative was to integrate artificial intelligence into the literature review process for a quality improvement group project to develop students’ ability to use artificial intelligence responsibly, ethically, and critically. This approach included validating the accuracy of artificial intelligence generated information. Methods: This initiative was offered as an honors conversion opportunity within the Clinical Science II course to undergraduate nursing students. Six students opted to participate and were divided into two groups of three. Groups selected a topic related to the course content and aligned it with one of the Joint Commission national patient safety goals. Groups developed a clinical question, search strategy, conducted a literature review, and used artificial intelligence to identify evidence. Results: Benefits of using artificial intelligence included the generation of creative ideas, provision of workflow steps, and a broad range of solutions. Challenges included a lack of concrete examples and a tendency for artificial intelligence generated information to be more practical than theoretical. Groups found artificial intelligence generated findings aligned with most articles from their literature reviews. Conclusions: Incorporating the utilization of artificial intelligence into nursing curriculums can help programs monitor usage while managing growing cohorts. Allowing students to engage with artificial intelligence under guided instruction enhances understanding of its practical applications in clinical settings. This will better prepare students for real-world practice while ensuring academic integrity is maintained.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The increasing demand for sustainable buildings and healthier indoor environments has transformed the role of Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) systems from conventional mechanical services into integral components of architectural and interior design strategies. Modern occupants spend a significant portion of their lives indoors, making indoor environmental quality (IEQ), thermal comfort, air quality, and energy efficiency essential considerations in contemporary living spaces. Traditionally, HVAC systems and interior design were developed as separate disciplines, often resulting in conflicts between aesthetic objectives, spatial functionality, and mechanical performance. However, recent approaches emphasize interdisciplinary collaboration between architects, interior designers, and HVAC engineers to create environments that are both environmentally responsible and occupant-centric. This review paper explores the integration of HVAC systems with interior design for achieving sustainable and comfortable living spaces. The study examines the influence of spatial planning, building materials, furniture arrangement, ventilation strategies, smart control technologies, and energy-efficient HVAC solutions on indoor comfort and sustainability. The paper discusses how emerging technologies such as Internet of Things (IoT)-based sensors, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven control systems, and building automation platforms enable adaptive environmental management. Furthermore, the research highlights the importance of considering HVAC requirements during the early stages of interior design development to optimize energy performance, improve indoor air quality, and enhance user experience. The integration of HVAC systems with interior design represents a multidisciplinary approach where technology, environmental responsibility, and human-centered design converge. Future sustainable interiors will depend on intelligent HVAC solutions that respond dynamically to occupant needs while minimizing energy consumption and environmental impact.
topics: Indoor Air Quality and Microbial Exposure

documents.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has transformed residential environments from conventional static spaces into intelligent, adaptive, and interconnected ecosystems. Smart home technologies integrating the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), sensor networks, cloud computing, and automated building services are increasingly influencing contemporary interior design practices. Unlike traditional interior design approaches that primarily focus on spatial aesthetics, functionality, and occupant comfort, smart interiors introduce dynamic interaction between users, architectural components, and automated environmental systems. This review critically examines the integration of smart home technologies into modern interior design with particular emphasis on automated building services, including intelligent lighting, smart heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC), security systems, energy management, automated shading, and adaptive furniture systems. A systematic literature review approach was adopted to analyse recent research from Scopus-indexed journals, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, and Taylor & Francis databases. The review identifies that smart home development has progressed from simple automation systems toward AI-driven adaptive environments capable of predicting occupant behaviour, optimizing energy consumption, and enhancing residential comfort. Smart lighting and HVAC systems demonstrate significant potential for reducing energy demand, while IoT-based monitoring platforms enable real-time management of indoor environmental quality. Furthermore, emerging technologies such as digital twins, edge computing, smart materials, and robotics are expected to redefine future interior design practices. However, several challenges remain, including interoperability limitations, cybersecurity risks, privacy concerns, high implementation costs, and insufficient integration between technology developers and design professionals. The paper argues that future smart interiors should adopt a human-centred approach where automation remains supportive rather than dominant. This review provides an interdisciplinary framework connecting interior design, building automation, artificial intelligence, and sustainable development, contributing to the emerging field of intelligent residential environments.

Virtual higher education seeks to address the growing demand for sustainable, inclusive, and ethical educational models within the context of digital transformation and the progressive integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI). The purpose of this study is to analyze the pedagogical, ethical, and organizational conditions required for the implementation of AI applications related to academic tutoring and student monitoring from the perspective of educational sustainability. The research adopts a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design. The quantitative phase consists of a questionnaire using Likert-scale items administered to students, faculty members, and academic tutors, followed by a qualitative phase based on semi-structured interviews aimed at exploring in greater depth the perceptions, experiences, and tensions identified during the quantitative stage. The discussion is structured around four key dimensions: institutional ethical governance, AI-supported academic tutoring, digital inclusion, and systematic evaluation. The findings suggest that AI can contribute to ensuring the continuity of students’ educational pathways, enhancing personalized learning experiences, and enabling the early identification of academic risks. However, it may also give rise to challenges related to privacy, algorithmic bias, surveillance, technological dependency, and the displacement of professional judgment. The study concludes that AI can effectively contribute to educational sustainability only if it is implemented as a transparent decision-support tool that complements, rather than replaces, human judgment while ensuring data protection, accessibility, faculty oversight, and institutional accountability.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Drug discovery and safety testing are complicated time-consuming processes marked by expensive nature and failure at late stage. Conventional experimental and animal methods tend to have low predictive validity and low human outcome translation. The latest advances in artificial intelligence, such as machine learning, deep learning, and data-driven modelling are changing the pharmaceutical value chain, as they allow to identify the target more efficiently, design the molecule, predictive pharmacology, and proactive safety assessment of the drug. This introductory chapter gives an overview of the development of drug discovery and toxicology towards AI-enabled paradigms. It analyses the principles of AI, the contribution of multimodal data integration, and the application in discovery, pharmacology, toxicology, and pharmacovigilance. The regulatory expectations, ethical considerations, and the existing issues pertaining to data quality, model interpretability, and clinical translation are also addressed in the chapter.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Maritime foundering is a low-frequency but high-consequence accident mode associated with multiple human, technical, supervisory, and organizational vulnerabilities. This study develops a data-driven framework integrating an adapted Human Factors Analysis and Classification System (HFACS), Apriori association rule mining, the Decision-Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL), and a Fuzzy Cognitive Map (FCM). A database of 155 foundering investigation reports from the China Maritime Safety Administration was coded into 50 risk factors. Apriori association mining identified empirical conditional associations in the coded reports, and their confidence values were used to parameterize the subsequent DEMATEL and FCM analyses. The modeled results distinguish highly activated terminal vulnerability accumulators from upstream intervention factors. Under the baseline FCM settings, idealized suppression of substandard physical and mental condition (P10), a lagging emergency response mechanism (O11), and the absence of an emergency preparedness plan (S8) yielded the largest reductions in aggregate activation across the remaining factors, with Global Sensitivity Index magnitudes of approximately 0.124–0.136. The findings support cross-level safety interventions that target latent organizational, supervisory, and preconditional vulnerabilities before they propagate into foundering.

Abstract The aim of this study is to explore motivational patterns in teacher candidates' cover letters (CL) and to examine the methodological role of artificial intelligence (AI) in qualitative content analysis. The theoretical framework is provided by the literature on teacher career motivation, qualitative text analysis, and the latest approaches to AI-based content analysis. The empirical analysis is based on the CLs of teacher training applicants. The analysis uses deductive coding, employing both human coders and an AI-based analytical system. The aim of the text analysis is to identify the dominant motivational factors and construct a motivational factor structure. The qualitative results are supplemented at an early stage by quantitative analysis, which examines the relationships between the identified motivational factors and the selected background variables. The methodological contribution of the study lies in the use of AI-assisted pre-coding within a deductive qualitative framework combined with systematic human validation. The results show that the most dominant motivational factors for teacher candidates are 1. Love of teaching, 2. Internal interest, 3. Shaping the next generation, 4. Career adjustment. Automated screening indicated that, on average, approximately 20% of the analysed text was flagged as potentially AI-generated. Potential AI-assisted writing may affect the linguistic and stylistic characteristics of the letters.

The increasing involvement of the emotional Artificial Intelligence and affective computing in child-oriented digital space has revolutionized the organization of persuasion, engagement and consumption. This chapter reviews mood-responsive marketing systems, which deduce and respond to the emotional state of children in real-time, a concept known as invisible persuasion to explain the influence of algorithmic marketing at the unconscious level. Basing the analysis on the interdisciplinary theory and recent case studies of educational platforms and smart toy ecosystems, the analysis indicates how the emotional inference, adaptive reward calibration, and loops of reinforcement influence engagement and dependency. The chapter points out the ethical, psychological and governance issues stating that AI design should be emotionally responsible, protecting the autonomy of children, their well-being, and limits of their development.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: We know that biology’s almost astronomical complexity can, in principle, be explained by the paradigm of natural selection, together with John Holland’s new paradigm of an emergent hierarchy of increasingly complex adaptive systems (CASs). This paper shows that these two paradigms might also explain conscious experience, an explanation that, though anticipated by the narratologist Bernini, has not heretofore been clarified. Paradigm shifts happen slowly. Current research on CASs mainly uses computer simulations and mathematics to explore the properties of existing CASs. This paper draws upon the well-understood hierarchy of biological CASs to propose its extension into a psychological hierarchy that includes narrative and hence, conscious experience. Psychoanalyst Daniel Stern’s observational studies show that, in human breast feeding, a narrative emerges from biology. As an infant, you internalized your care-giver’s experience of you to initiate your experience of yourself. Observational studies of adults in therapy groups further argue that conscious experience is a CAS that emerges from interacting narratives. Clark and Chalmers showed that the brain has developed cultural artifacts to extend its capacity, examples being music, language, and narrative. Therefore consciousness would also be a cultural artifact. Current neuroscientific theories of consciousness (ToCs), limited by Crick’s materialist ‘astonishing hypothesis,’ seek to explain consciousness in terms of neural processing. This paper’s relational hypothesis is more plausible. This paper’s ToC overlaps with three out of Seth and Bayne’s (2023) four main classes of neuroscientific ToCs. It meets Seth and Bayne’s criteria for support by making two confirmed predictions, one about autism, the other about dreams (autism and dreams both disturb experience), that the four classes of neuroscientific ToCs fail to make. This paper’s ToC has implications for the development of artificial intelligence.

In this chapter, the authors further develop on the changing face with regard to the juvenile consumer within the fast-growing realm of artificial intelligence. It also shows how AI technologies, including smart devices, social networking recommendation systems, and the Internet of Toys are shifting children as passive participants of the marketing process to active and data-generating participants in the digital economy. The paper is interdisciplinary and combines the knowledge of marketing, developmental psychology, digital ethics, and public policy to discuss four key issues, such as AI-enabled marketing practices, privacy, data ownership, digital well-being, and regulation. The authors state that, as much as AI presents opportunities of personalized learning and creative play and enhances connectivity. The growing popularity of gamification, influencer marketing, and emotionally adaptive systems makes the distinctions between entertainment and advertising and makes children less aware of when they are being sold a product.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: University classrooms are where students acquire higher-level knowledge and develop skills for future professional development in a work environment that requires decision-making through analysis, synthesis, and evaluation. Artificial intelligence provides guidance to students as a support tool, but there is a risk that it may become invasive or substitute for solving, thinking, and dictating what should or can be done, resulting in negative impacts and generating significant risks. The objective is to investigate students' reflections of artificial intelligence for their proper training, which must consciously consider sustainability and the importance of the philosophy of science to position it as a technological advancement. The paradigm is qualitative, as it involves discussion and the speculative aspects of the philosophy of science. Worksheets and a Likert scale were used to collect information. The results show that approximately 35% of respondents agree on the positive and negative aspects of its use, highlighting risks and benefits. The most radical position, which defends artificial intelligence, is held by a very small percentage of the total respondents.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the convergence of extended reality and artificial intelligence in language education, focusing on immersive conversational agents. While XR-AI technologies offer notable affective and linguistic benefits for learners, the evolving responsibilities of teachers are frequently overlooked. To address this gap, this chapter investigates shifting educator roles through three conceptual pillars: a sociomaterial perspective, human-centered design thinking, and the human-in-the-loop principle. By synthesizing these core pillars with current research, the author proposes the Entangled Design Loop (EDL) framework. This pedagogical model outlines the actions teachers must take before, within, and beyond immersive environments. Ultimately, this framework equips language educators with actionable strategies for integrating smart technologies while ensuring that pedagogical decision-making remains decisively human.

The electronic health record (EHR) comprises structured and unstructured data, both of which are integral for comprehensively representing patient history. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has enabled the incorporation of unstructured data modalities into machine learning models that leverage EHR data. In this systematic review, we characterize studies that utilize LLM-enabled multimodal predictive modeling with EHR data. Following a screening of 641 studies, 57 met inclusion criteria. We identified three strategies for LLM-based multimodal integration: embedding, extraction, and text fusion. Delineated by the format of the unstructured data at the time of fusion, all strategies yielded performance gains (average 6.4% increase) over single modality models. LLMs facilitated modeling by generating note-embeddings for downstream prediction, extracting clinically informative variables, and summarizing long text documents prior to integration. Building on our review, we identified LLM-enhanced predictive modeling considerations that include sample size, interpretability, and computational costs. This study supports the potential value of LLMs for EHR-based predictive modeling and provides a framework for future multimodal modeling tools.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The Hopfield model, originally inspired by spin glasses, occupies a central place at the intersection of statistical mechanics, neural networks, and artificial intelligence. Despite its conceptual simplicity and broad applicability, it is rarely integrated into the undergraduate physics curriculum. We present the Hopfield model as a pedagogically rich framework that naturally unifies core topics from the undergraduate physics curriculum and that provides a concise introduction based on concepts such as a model's energy function, dynamics, and pattern stability. We discuss practical aspects of its simulation and provide simulation codes. We also propose problems designed to mirror research practice, which can be included in undergraduate classes.

Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved notable success in closed‐set classification of neurodegenerative diseases, but its performance degrades significantly in more realistic open‐set settings, such as discovering rare or novel disease subtypes from unlabeled data that are not seen during training. Purpose This study introduces, to our knowledge, the first framework for generalized category discovery (GCD) in neurodegenerative diseases using MRI. It aims to leverage labeled data from known categories to automatically identify novel categories within unlabeled datasets. Methods We propose a GCD framework integrating semi‐supervised contrastive learning with global‐local representation learning to jointly optimize feature learning. Globally, we enforce consistency between weakly augmented views of the same instance by aligning their similarity relationships with other embeddings in a support queue. Locally, we treat neighborhood embeddings from the support queue as positive pairs for cross‐instance contrastive learning, enhancing fine‐grained discrimination. This dual strategy results in a unified learning objective that is applicable to both labeled and unlabeled data, effectively narrowing the representation gap among semantically similar instances. Results We evaluate our method on a benchmark dataset comprising six neurodegenerative diseases, with over 1500 patient samples. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms representative state‐of‐the‐art methods. Specifically, our method achieves 66.02% Accuracy and 60.59% Normalized Mutual Information on all categories, and 54.53% Accuracy and 16.67% Normalized Mutual Information on novel categories, surpassing existing state‐of‐the‐art methods. Conclusions Our framework underscores the model's robustness and its practical value in discovering new neurodegenerative disease conditions, highlighting its potential for advancing open‐set diagnostic AI.

This article focuses on the legal challenges arising from the use of artificial intelligence in healthcare from the perspective of global health policy. While the active application of AI at various stages of healthcare demonstrates increasing efficiency, it also increases legal risks and highlights the necessity of an adapted legal framework. The article argues that the integration of artificial intelligence in healthcare is more challenging from a legal perspective than from a technological or ethical point of view, as it actively raises issues such as patient rights, the principle of informed consent, liability, and other related concerns, requiring coherent regulatory standards and coordinated policy responses. The authors propose a human-centered governance model that ensures the best possible balance, protects human rights and minimizes legal challenges arising from AI-related outcomes.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study investigates the impact of a legal regulation that relaxes mandatory attendance requirements in university courses in certain German states on academic practices. This study employed a descriptive design within a qualitative framework. The study group comprised six academics affiliated with Johannes Gutenberg University in Germany during the 2023–2024 academic year. Data were collected through semi-structured online interviews and analyzed using descriptive methods. The findings reveal that the legal regulation operates within a multi-layered structure. First, it was determined that higher education policies vary among the states in accordance with Germany’s federal structure, and that participation policies are shaped within this decentralized governance framework. Second, the emergence of the regulation was influenced by the positioning of students as autonomous and adult individuals, as well as by political and institutional pressure dynamics. Third, regulation enhances student autonomy and self-regulation skills, supports intrinsic motivation, and fosters innovation and academic competition in teaching processes. However, it was also determined that the regulation has led to significant negative consequences, such as a decline in faculty motivation, weakened classroom interaction, reduced course quality, and a diminished sense of responsibility among students. In conclusion, this study demonstrates that attendance policies in higher education encompass both pedagogical opportunities and structural risks, highlighting the necessity of balanced policies that strike a balance between student autonomy and the quality of teaching processes.

The application of artificial intelligence (AI) to education and policy-making offers them both hotly awaited possibilities and urgent ethical concerns. This conceptual paper, aims to understand how ethical AI models can drive data-informed decision-making that is in line with sustainability missions, ethical research practices and procedures. Though AI holds untapped tools for analyzing complex data, introducing prognosatory potential, and assisting policy creation, the paper negates that unchecked use might actually perpetuate biases, and foster irresponsibility and loss of transparency which will weakenedsocieties..A conceptual framework is developed in the paper that situates ethical AI as a connecting point between raw data and actionable decisions in the subject area of policy and research education. Using cutting-edge paradigms from data sciences, sustainability studies and educational literature: The pillars of the framework are four: (1) fairness and accountability of algorithmic models; (2) inclusion in data representations with stakeholders; (3) transparency in decision-making; and (4) outcomes towards sustainability for long-term social and ecological welfare..By incorporating these pillars into both policy and research education, the research identifies how institutions could guide their future African leaders and researchers to provide them with the competences to think critically with AI while ensuring ethical protection. The paper is further used to show how the adoption of ethical AI improves the legitimacy of evidence-based policymaking and is used to support changes in educational practices aimed on instilling responsibility through innovation. Informatics Research: This study adds to the ongoing discussion on the governance of AI, by presenting design frameworks based on education and policy that embedding ethics in the design of data-driven system itself. Ultimately, the study calls for human-centered approach to AI, which not only helps make decisions faster but also ensures that the technological advancements are on the path for sustainable and socially responsible futures.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Computational or machine ethics examines how morality could be implemented in machines and represented computationally. In the cognitive sciences, different architectures (rule-based and connectionist) have been proposed. Nevertheless, such approaches have limitations when incorporating ethical claims. With the rise of artificial intelligence, new ways of simulating moral expertise seem possible, where chatbots can serve as dialogue partners for moral orientation. However, as I will argue, such systems lack a theoretical grounding in metaethics, as do the former approaches. In order to align such systems ethically and ground them conceptually, a topography of moral competence must be developed. By outlining this topography, I will show some directions for further research and how such systems might enhance us morally.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are now widely used to produce and support digital content such as stories, news items and social-media posts. Such tools can make a single piece of output look better, yet they also bring worries about originality, sameness across many outputs, bias, factual accuracy, creative control and ownership rights. This paper reviews five chosen scholarly works that look at creator responsibility, AI-supported story writing, prompting as a creative method, copyright, and bias in machine-written news. Read together, the studies indicate that a gain for one writer does not automatically become a gain for everyone: stories written with AI help may score higher while growing more alike. The remaining works point to the need for human fact-checking, the risk of skewed representation, the difficulty of turning unspoken creative know-how into written prompts, and unsettled questions about ownership and openness. We compare how the studies were carried out and what each contributes, draw out the shared challenges, and suggest where future work could head. Because only five hand-picked papers were examined and no exhaustive database search was run, this work is a focused narrative review rather than a systematic one.

documents.abstract: Patient-facing drug-delivery information must communicate pharmaceutical facts in language that readers can understand and act upon safely.The present interdisciplinary study examines generative artificial intelligence (AI) as a controlled linguistic-optimization tool for improving the readability and patient-centred presentation of drug-delivery information while preserving pharmaceutical meaning.A document-based comparative design was developed around 24 patient-facing passages representing oral modified-release, transdermal, inhaled, injectable, topical and medication-safety communication.Original and AI-assisted versions were evaluated using readability, sentence-length, lexical-complexity, terminology and content-fidelity measures.For the pilot analysis presented here, the mean Flesch Reading Ease score increased from 47.8 ± 8.9 to 68.6 ± 7.1, while the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level decreased from 11.62 ± 2.14 to 7.34 ± 1.18.Mean word count decreased from 286.4 ± 72.5 to 219.7 ± 61.3 words.Patient-centredness increased from 2.71 ± 0.54 to 4.42 ± 0.38 on a fivepoint scale.Content fidelity, safety completeness and terminology accuracy remained high at 95.1%, 94.6% and 93.8%, respectively, but were not perfect.These findings indicate that generative AI can substantially reduce linguistic burden and improve the organization of patient-facing drug-delivery information, while also demonstrating why expert pharmaceutical verification is necessary.The study provides a practical research model for English Departments to contribute to pharmaceutical communication through corpus linguistics, readability analysis, terminology management and AI-assisted language evaluation.The results should be interpreted as a pilot benchmark until the complete source corpus, coding sheets and independent verification are archived with the final study.

documents.abstract: Evaluation practice often faces a trade-off between depth and metrics, frequently resulting in the marginalisation of local voices. Traditional methods of coding texts, such as interviews, risk filtering diverse narratives through pre-defined, donor-driven frameworks, perpetuating a form of epistemic violence that prioritises ‘data’ over ‘story’. We propose an alternative: AI-assisted causal mapping as a method for ‘listening at scale’ using a zero-codebook approach where Generative AI serves as a ‘low-level’ assistant to extract causal links from large volumes of unstructured text without an imposed codebook. A case study of Tree Aid in Burkina Faso demonstrates how this method reveals complex outcomes which might be missed by models that use a pre-determined codebook. We introduce ‘soft recoding’ as a technique to align local narratives with donors’ conceptual frameworks without erasing original data. We conclude by reflecting on the tensions between bottom-up storytelling and top-down accountability, arguing that while AI has its own biases, rigorous human oversight can use it to amplify rather than silence marginalised voices.

Technology flow (TF) forecasting aims to predict whether a technology will be utilized by another, which is significant for future cross-integration technology innovation. Although existing methods have made substantial progress in intra-domain TF forecasting, inter-domain TF forecasting remains underexplored and faces several fundamental challenges. Specifically, semantic gaps between technologies from different domains hinder effective representation learning; historical inter-domain TFs are highly sparse, limiting the ability to learn reliable structural dependencies; and intra-domain and inter-domain TFs exhibit distinct flow patterns, which are difficult to model within a unified framework. To address these challenges, in this paper, we propose an LLM-enhanced Graph Contrastive Learning ( LGCL ) framework that supports both intra-domain and inter-domain TF forecasting. Specifically, we first leverage LLMs with bias-aware representation adjustment to generate semantically enriched and accurate technology representations to bridge gaps across multiple domains. Then, to mitigate the sparsity of inter-domain TF data, a technology co-occurrence view is incorporated to complement historical TF information. We further develop a non-negative contrastive learning module to integrate the TF and co-occurrence views, enabling effective representation alignment without relying on negative samples. In addition, we design decoupled loss functions to separately supervise intra-domain and inter-domain flows, mitigating the difficulty of jointly modeling their different flow patterns under a unified objective. Finally, experiments on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of our approach and provide valuable insights into future technology flow trends. Our code is available at https://github.com/huijieliu2023/LGCL .

Antibiotic resistance is a mounting global public health and development threat, with the misuse and overuse of antibiotics driving the rapid dissemination of multidrug-resistant pathogens. Developing next-generation small-molecule antibiotics requires in-depth investigation of resistance mechanisms and the identification of novel targets to overcome the limitations of current treatments. However, current strategies mainly rely on sequence-based homology search or models trained on manually curated datasets, which often suffer from outdated annotations, limited coverage, and high false-positive rates. These limitations hinder the identification of novel resistance targets. To address these limitations, we developed a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered automated pipeline that systematically mines resistance-related knowledge from full-text publications and supplementary materials, thereby supporting scalable and iterative data integration. Building on this framework, we constructed AResDB , a curated resource that integrates data from over 8570 published papers covering bacterial species, compounds, genes, mutations, phenotypes, and quantitative measurements. On this foundation, we constructed AResKG , a large-scale, multi-species knowledge graph of antibiotic resistance integrating 14 entity types, 27 relation types, and over 52.1 million triples. Experimental results based on AResKG demonstrate its effectiveness in improving the performance of commonly used machine learning methods for predicting gene-antibiotic resistance, compared with existing knowledge graphs. This work establishes a scalable, LLM-powered framework for antibiotic resistance research that advances the understanding of resistance mechanisms and accelerates the discovery of next-generation therapeutics.

Kinematic modeling and path planning are critical problems in intelligent automation that directly affect the precision, adaptability, and safety of robotic arms. The ever-growing complexity of manipulators, including redundant DOFs, unique kinematic architectures, and environmental dynamics, has highlighted the drawbacks of classic analytical and Jacobian approaches in handling singularities, computational costs, and generalizability. Despite many reviews addressing particular problems such as inverse kinematics or reinforcement learning, an extensive overview of methodological development is yet to be provided. The sources for the literature review were mainly obtained from Google Scholar, while the publishing details for the selected articles were then cross-checked using the individual publishers’ and journal sites. The sources are divided into the following nine categories: analytical and hybrid inverse kinematics, neural networks, optimization, deep reinforcement learning, sampling- and learning-based motion planning, diffusion models, trajectory optimization, obstacle avoidance, and imitation learning. From the review, it is evident that there is a shift from traditional approaches such as analysis and optimization to AI-based methods like neural networks, deep reinforcement learning, and diffusion-based systems, with 105 studies published between 2022 and 2026. Some of the findings include MLP-based inverse kinematics (R2 > 0.99), meta-heuristic optimization resulting in a 4.75 × 10−4 cm position error, a 99.4% path-planning success rate through reinforcement learning, diffusion-based visuomotor control, and challenges facing intelligent robotic manipulation research.

This chapter presents the development of machine learning models for short-term energy demand forecasting in academic buildings, using a dataset from a higher education campus in Portugal. The dataset comprises quarter-hourly power demand data collected between January 2016 and February 2020, along with relevant exogenous variables. The study focuses on the impact of hyperparameter tuning on model performance, applying various algorithms—including Random Forest, Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines, Artificial Neural Network, and Support Vector Machines. Grid Search and Random Search techniques were employed to optimize each model’s hyperparameters. Performance was evaluated using benchmarking metrics and visualization tools such as daily load profiles and scatter plots. The results indicate that the Random Forest and Artificial Neural Network models outperformed the others, particularly during school days and examination periods, which represent the most active times on campus. Beyond its technical contributions, this chapter illustrates how machine learning-based forecasting can support energy-aware decision-making in academic buildings, contributing to more efficient and sustainable campus operations. Moreover, the case study presented here highlights the pedagogical potential of integrating AI tools into sustainability curricula, fostering interdisciplinary learning and providing students and researchers with practical insights into the application of artificial intelligence in real-world energy systems.

Trained machine learning models can hold on to traces of the data they were built from, including personal, outdated, incorrect, or unauthorized records. Deleting an entry from a database does not erase what a model has already absorbed from it. Machine unlearning tackles this gap by lowering or removing the effect of chosen training data, ideally without retraining the whole model every time. This review looks at five studies published between 2021 and 2025: one on coded machine unlearning, one on neuron masking, one on zero-shot unlearning, and two wider surveys of methods and evaluation. Together they trace a path from partition-based training designs and changes to model structure toward techniques that still work after the original training samples are gone, accompanied by increasingly systematic taxonomies and metrics. We compare the studies on the data access they assume, the unlearning strategy they use, their efficiency, how well they preserve utility, and how forgetting is verified. We also discuss the main open problems: the absence of a universal evaluation standard, the tension between forgetting and keeping performance on retained tasks, the risk of leftover information, and the difficulty of carrying these methods over to large language models and live systems. The work is a focused narrative review of the chosen papers; no new experiments or benchmark results are claimed. Our conclusion is that machine unlearning is a promising tool for privacy and model governance, but dependable use in practice requires measurable forgetting, clearly stated assumptions, and independent verification.

documents.abstract: The use of Conversational Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is growing as a way to interact with health information, especially for the public. This theory-based conceptual synthesis suggests a multilevel governance approach to reducing the likelihood for generated information to become unsafe action – GenAI health information resilience (GenAI-HIR). Its contribution is immediately usable and practical — deploying organizations and public-health actors and public-health actors can use the consequence-based control tiers, actor-specific safeguards, and domain-level audit anchors, and the proposed competency configuration still needs to be validated and is a research agenda for the future. Five conceptually distinct functions at the individual and workforce levels describe at which point protection may contribute to the decision pathway, but are not necessarily assumed to be empirically separable: recognize, interrogate, verify, contextualize, and escalate. Organizational capacity is limited to controls particular to created health information such as authorized sources, attainable human routing, incident monitoring and corrective action. Platform and regulatory conditions are constraints, safety, access, calibrated trust, and equity, outcomes. The framework was created using an expert guided purposive synthesis of the 62 sources that were retained, not a systematic review process. It distinguishes between an explanatory risk model and a normative control architecture and categorizes outputs with respect to type of output, severity, urgency, reversibility, context dependence, mitigation feasibility, and remaining risk. Falsification criteria are now included in six propositions. The candidate self-report indicators are kept as material for the cognitive interviewing only and must be correlated with behavioral vignettes before use for psychometric purposes. GenAI-HIR is therefore not a validated scale, certification standard or replacement for accessible professional care; it is a model for competency that can be falsified in future research and a governance structure that can be audited for current implementation.

documents.abstract: Human rights have become a pervasive vocabulary in Indian legal and social science research, yet the structure and direction of this expanding literature have rarely been examined systematically. This review maps 457 Scopus-indexed journal articles on human rights with at least one Indian institutional affiliation, published between 2016 and 2026, using performance analysis and science-mapping techniques. Annual output grew more than five-fold, from 14 articles in 2016 to 75 in 2025 and 82 in 2026, a compound annual growth rate of about 20.5 per cent. The literature is highly dispersed: the 457 articles appeared in 318 journals, 36 of which account for one-third of the output, and 93 per cent of the 1,516 authors contributed only one article. Citation impact is modest (median one citation; 36.3 per cent uncited; dataset h-index 22). Keyword co-occurrence analysis identifies six principal clusters: constitutional equality and discrimination; public health, pandemic and surveillance; artificial intelligence and intellectual property; climate change, displacement and the rights of nature; data protection and international law; and sustainable development and consumer protection. Thematic evolution shows a shift from trade-related intellectual property and health policy in 2016-2020 to COVID-19 and constitutional dignity in 2021-2023, and to artificial intelligence, data protection and climate change in 2024-2026. In contrast, the institutions through which rights are enforced receive very little attention: police, prisons and custody appear in about 2 per cent of articles, caste and Dalit concerns in 2.2 per cent, and the National Human Rights Commission in only three articles (0.7 per cent), none of which takes a commission as its object of study. The review argues that Indian human rights scholarship has undergone a “technological and regulatory turn” that risks neglecting the accountability of the coercive state, and proposes a research agenda centred on enforcement institutions, caste and gender intersections, and data-driven evaluation.

The introduction of innovative products is a critical driver of competitive advantage in highly turbulent technological environments. The objective of this article is to systematically analyze the recent literature on the marketing strategies that optimize the acceptance and performance of such innovations. Using a systematic-narrative methodology, a final corpus of 20 scientific articles published between 2020 and 2025 in high-impact databases such as Scopus and Web of Science was selected. The results reveal that commercial success does not reside exclusively in technical superiority, but in the creative configuration of an integrated marketing mix, where packaging design, dynamic pricing, and the diversification of channels toward e-commerce reduce adoption barriers. A strategic shift is identified, moving from traditional launch models toward agile, iterative, and niche approaches that prioritize user co-creation to mitigate perceived risk. Furthermore, functional communication and educational pre-announcements emerge as essential cognitive mechanisms for reducing consumer resistance to change in the face of radical innovations. It is concluded that dynamic organizational capabilities, enhanced by Marketing 4.0 and artificial intelligence, are crucial for personalizing the value proposition and ensuring product sustainability in global markets.

The development of digital technology has enabled the emergence and expansion of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs), which are transforming education through global accessibility, flexibility, and interactivity. This paper analyzes several platforms, their structure, the role of mentors, and the application of learning analytics. By searching citation databases and using generative artificial intelligence tools, relevant studies in the field were identified as the foundation of the analysis. An analysis of the most prominent MOOC platforms was conducted, with a more detailed comparison between the international platforms Coursera, edX, Future Learn, and the Croatian national platforms Srce and CARNET. The research shows that platforms differ in their use of technology, target groups, and approaches to mentorship, but they share a common goal: to provide accessible and personalized education. Personalized education is maintained through the role of mentors, reflected in communication on forums, AI assistants, and peer interaction. Learning analytics also play an equally important role, enabling precise monitoring of progress and adapting content to the specific needs of individuals. Alongside many advantages, the paper also discusses challenges such as privacy protection and data accuracy, which influence the development of MOOCs.
